name: Diclofenac
route_note: Oral tablets and capsules; topical gel and solution; medicated patch; injection; suppositories; eye drops.

discovery.by: Alfred Sallmann and Rudolf Pfister, Ciba-Geigy
discovery.note: Designed to combine structural features thought to give potent anti-inflammatory activity with good tolerability.

rx_status: prescription; topical and low-dose oral OTC in many countries
tagline: Widely used NSAID whose veterinary use devastated South Asian vultures
summary: Diclofenac is a potent NSAID used orally, topically and by injection for arthritis, musculoskeletal pain and inflammation. It carries a higher cardiovascular risk than some other NSAIDs, and its veterinary use caused a catastrophic decline of vultures in South Asia.
mechanism: Diclofenac inhibits COX-1 and COX-2, with relative selectivity for COX-2 similar to celecoxib in some assays, reducing prostaglandin synthesis.
Its COX-2 preference may contribute to its cardiovascular risk. Topical formulations deliver drug to superficial joints with much lower systemic exposure.

history.title: Vulture link
history.detail: Oaks et al. (Nature) show that diclofenac residues in livestock carcasses cause fatal kidney failure in Gyps vultures.

history.title: Veterinary ban
history.detail: India, Pakistan and Nepal ban veterinary diclofenac.

history.title: Topical gel
history.detail: Voltaren Gel 1% is approved in the US.

history.title: EU cardiovascular restrictions
history.detail: The EMA contraindicates systemic diclofenac in established heart failure, ischaemic heart disease and cerebrovascular disease.

history.title: US OTC gel
history.detail: Voltaren Arthritis Pain gel becomes available over the counter in the US.

safety.boxed_warning: Cardiovascular thrombotic events (myocardial infarction, stroke) and serious gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration and perforation; contraindicated for pain after coronary artery bypass graft surgery (US NSAID class boxed warning).

facts: Populations of three Gyps vulture species in South Asia fell by more than 95% from the 1990s, largely because of diclofenac in livestock carcasses.
